烏克蘭蘇爾瑪號是一種源自高加索地區或土耳其的雙簧管樂器，其名稱與該地區的祖爾納和: The Ukrainian surma is a double-reed instrument that comes from the Caucasus or Turkey, and its name is close to that of traditional instruments of the region such as the zurna and the surnay. After it reached Ukraine in the Middle Ages it was widely used in the Cossack armies and became an important part of military music. The surma is made of wood, with a conical bore and fingerholes, a bell at one end and a double reed at the other; it usually has nine or ten fingerholes and can produce chromatic notes by changing the force of the blowing. As Ukrainian national culture developed, the surma became part of the folk music tradition, and the term is also used for similar instruments such as wooden horns. The instrument bears witness to the rich mixture of musical cultures in Eastern Europe and reflects the spread of instruments along the Silk Road.

One end has a bell of wood or ivory, the other a pair of double reeds of cane or bamboo. The fingerholes are carved from the same wood, nine or ten of them. The body usually has nine or ten fingerholes, and the player can control the volume by changes of force and produce semitones. Compared with an ordinary horn it sounds by the vibration of a double reed; among Ukrainian folk instruments it comes in treble, alto and bass sizes, so that timbre and register differ.
The surma is an aerophone of the oboe family, Hornbostel–Sachs 422.112. It is a wooden body with a conical bore, a bell at one end and a double reed at the other, usually with nine or ten fingerholes; it can produce semitones and its timbre changes with the force of the blowing. It was widely used in the Cossack armies and is related to similar instruments in the Caucasus and Turkey; today it appears in Ukrainian folk instrument line-ups in treble, alto and bass sizes.
